dryRun.title: How React finds your state: hooks are a list, matched by call order
rows: if a hook is skipped by an if
dryRun.note: React stores hook data in a list per component and matches it by call order. So: call hooks only at the top level of a component or custom hook — never inside if, loops, nested functions or after an early return.

think.q:
function C({ on }) {
  const [a] = useState('a')
  if (on) { useState('b') }
  return <p>{a}</p>
}
why: The second render calls one more hook than the first, and React detects it: "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render."

think.q: if (!user) return null; const [x, setX] = useState(0). What is wrong?
opts: The hook is skipped on renders that return early, so the hook order changes
why: Move all hooks above any early return.

think.q: Where may you call useState?
opts: Inside a for loop with a fixed count
At the top level of a function component or a custom hook (a function starting with "use")
why: The use prefix lets the lint rule check custom hooks too.

think.q: Which hook-like call MAY appear inside an if in React 19?
why: use() is special-cased to be callable conditionally; every other hook is not.

think.q: What catches rule breaks before they run?
why: Turn it on in every React project.

try.task: Write a custom hook useToggle(initial = false) returning [on, toggle, setOn]. toggle must flip the latest value even when called twice in one handler.
examples: toggle(); toggle() in one handler → back to false
try.hint: Hooks at the top level; toggle uses the updater form.

checks.t: two toggles in one batch cancel out

takeaway.key: Hooks are matched by call order: only at the top level of components and custom hooks. Let the lint rule enforce it.
mistakes: Hooks after an early return.
Hooks inside if or loops.

dryRun.title: const [items, setItems] = useState(() => load())
rows: runs the initializer, stores the result
returns the stored value, ignores the argument
stores next if !Object.is(old, next), schedules render
dryRun.note: useState returns the value for this render and a setter. The initial argument is used only once (pass a function for expensive setup). Updates are compared with Object.is: setting the same value (or the same mutated object) does nothing.

think.q:
let calls = 0
const load = () => (calls++, [1, 2])
function C() { const [x, setX] = useState(load()); const [y, setY] = useState(load); return <button onClick={() => setX([...x])}>go</button> }
why: useState(load()) calls load on every render (3 renders = 3 calls); useState(load) calls it once. Total 4.

await mount(<C />)
await click($('button'))
await click($('button'))
console.log(calls)

think.q:
function C() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0)
  console.log('render', n)
  return <button onClick={() => setN(0)}>x</button>
}
why: Setting the same value bails out: no re-render.

think.q:
function C() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: 'a' })
  return <button onClick={() => setUser({ ...user, name: 'b' })}>{user.name}</button>
}
why: A new object (spread) is a new reference, so React re-renders with it.

think.q: Why does setN(n + 1); console.log(n) log the old value?
opts: n is a constant for this render; the setter only schedules the next render
why: Think of each render as a snapshot.

think.q: A form has 6 related fields that often change together. Better?
opts: One object in useState (or useReducer), updated immutably
why: Group state that changes together; split unrelated state.

try.task: Write useUndoState(initial) returning { value, set, undo, canUndo }: set pushes the old value to a history, undo restores the previous one.
examples: canUndo is false at the start
try.hint: Keep { past: [], value } in one useState so both change together.

checks.t: undo goes back step by step
two sets in one batch keep both steps

takeaway.key: Each render sees a snapshot. Lazy initializer for expensive setup, updater for "based on previous", new references for objects and arrays.
mistakes: useState(expensive()) recomputing every render.
Mutating state objects.

dryRun.title: Counter: mount → click → unmount
dryRun.note: Effects run after React updates the screen. The cleanup of the previous run happens before the next run and on unmount, and it still sees its own render's values. Effects synchronise with something outside React (timers, subscriptions, the network, the DOM).

think.q:
function Child() { console.log('render Child'); useEffect(() => console.log('effect Child')); return null }
function Parent() { console.log('render Parent'); useEffect(() => console.log('effect Parent')); return <Child /> }
opts: render Parent effect Parent render Child effect Child
render Parent render Child effect Parent effect Child
render Parent render Child effect Child effect Parent
render Child render Parent effect Parent effect Child
why: Render goes top-down, effects run bottom-up: a parent effect can rely on its children being mounted.

think.q: function App() { console.log('render'); useEffect(() => { console.log('effect'); return () => console.log('cleanup') }, []); return null }
why: In development StrictMode mounts, unmounts and mounts again to check your cleanup.
think.exec:
import { useState, useEffect, useLayoutEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, StrictMode, Fragment, Suspense, useTransition, useDeferredValue, startTransition, use, lazy, forwardRef, useImperativeHandle, Component } from 'react'
import { createPortal, flushSync } from 'react-dom'
function App() { console.log('render'); useEffect(() => { console.log('effect'); return () => console.log('cleanup') }, []); return null }
await mount(<StrictMode><App /></StrictMode>)

think.q:
function Ticker() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 10)
    return () => clearInterval(id)
  }, [])
  return <p>{count}</p>
}
why: With [] deps the interval keeps the first render's count (0), so it sets 1 forever. Use setCount((c) => c + 1).

think.q: An effect fetches results using query and page. Which deps?
why: List every reactive value the effect reads. The lint rule exhaustive-deps does this for you.

think.q: Typing fast fires 3 fetches and an old response arrives last. Fix?
opts: In cleanup, set an "ignore" flag (or abort the request) so a stale response is dropped
why: Each effect run cancels the previous one through its cleanup.

try.task: Write useDebouncedValue(value, ms): return value, but only after it has stopped changing for ms. Clean up the timer.
examples: typing "a","ab","abc" quickly → q updates once to "abc"
try.hint: useState(value); useEffect with setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), ms) and return () => clearTimeout(id); deps [value, ms].

checks.t: a new value restarts the timer (cleanup ran)

takeaway.key: Effects run after paint, bottom-up. Cleanup runs before the next run and on unmount. List every value the effect reads in deps; use updaters to avoid stale state.
mistakes: Missing deps → stale values.
No cleanup → leaking timers, subscriptions and late responses.
Using an effect to compute something you could compute during render.

dryRun.title: const renders = useRef(0); renders.current++
dryRun.note: useRef gives a mutable box { current } that survives renders. Changing it does not re-render. Use it for DOM nodes, timer ids, previous values and anything you need to remember but not show.

think.q:
function C() {
  const r = useRef(0)
  const [, force] = useState(0)
  return <><button onClick={() => { r.current++ }}>inc</button><button onClick={() => force((x) => x + 1)}>show</button><p>{r.current}</p></>
}
why: Changing ref.current does not re-render. The next render (from state) shows the latest value.

think.q:
function C() {
  const ref = useRef(null)
  console.log('render', ref.current === null)
  useEffect(() => console.log('effect', ref.current.tagName))
  return <input ref={ref} />
}
why: During the first render the DOM node does not exist yet; it is attached before effects run.

think.q:
function usePrevious(v) { const r = useRef(); useEffect(() => { r.current = v }); return r.current }
function C() { const [n, setN] = useState(1); const prev = usePrevious(n); return <button onClick={() => setN(n * 10)}>{n}/{String(prev)}</button> }
why: The effect saves the value after render, so during the next render the ref still holds the previous one.

think.q: Which belongs in a ref, not state?
opts: A setInterval id you need for clearInterval
The text shown in a heading
why: If changing it should not update the screen, a ref is right.

think.q: Why should you avoid reading or writing ref.current during render (except for lazy init)?
opts: Refs are not tracked: the UI will not update and renders become impure
why: Read refs in effects and handlers.

try.task: Write usePrevious(value) (the value from the previous render, undefined at first) and useRenderCount() (how many times the component has rendered, without causing renders).
try.hint: usePrevious: store in a ref inside useEffect, return ref.current. useRenderCount: increment a ref during render (it never causes a render).

checks.t: render count goes up with each render

takeaway.key: useRef = a box that survives renders and never triggers one. For DOM nodes, ids, previous values; not for anything you show.
mistakes: Expecting the UI to update when ref.current changes.
Reading a DOM ref during the first render.

dryRun.title: Tooltip that must sit above its button
rows: tooltip at the wrong place, then jumps
dryRun.note: useLayoutEffect runs after the DOM is updated but before the browser paints, so you can measure and adjust without a visible flicker. It blocks painting, so use it only for measure-then-position work; everything else belongs in useEffect.

think.q:
function C() {
  console.log('render')
  useEffect(() => console.log('effect'))
  useLayoutEffect(() => console.log('layout'))
  return null
}
why: Layout effects run first, right after the DOM update; normal effects later.

import { createPortal, flushSync } from 'react-dom'

think.q:
function C() {
  const [w, setW] = useState(0)
  const log = useRef([])
  log.current.push(w)
  useLayoutEffect(() => { if (w === 0) setW(120) }, [w])
  useEffect(() => { if (w === 120) console.log(log.current.join(',')) })
  return <div style={{ width: w }} />
}
why: The state set in the layout effect causes a synchronous re-render before paint, so the user never sees width 0.

think.q: Which needs useLayoutEffect?
opts: Measuring an element's size to position a popover next to it
why: Only DOM measurement that must affect the very first paint.

think.q: What happens with useLayoutEffect during server rendering?
opts: It does not run on the server (there is no layout); React warns in older versions
why: Do layout work only on the client.

think.q: Why not use useLayoutEffect everywhere?
opts: It runs synchronously before paint, so slow code there delays what the user sees
why: useEffect lets the browser paint first.

try.task: Write useElementWidth() returning [ref, width]: attach ref to an element and get its getBoundingClientRect().width, measured in a layout effect (before paint).
examples: in the test, getBoundingClientRect is mocked to 240 → w === 240

checks.t: returns a ref and a number
the measured width is there before effects (no flicker frame)

takeaway.key: useLayoutEffect = measure and adjust the DOM before paint (no flicker). Everything else: useEffect.
mistakes: Using layout effects for data fetching.
Heavy work in layout effects delaying paint.

think.q: When is useReducer a better fit than useState?
opts: Several pieces of state change together through named events (add, remove, clear)
why: A reducer documents every way the state can change.

think.q: Is dispatch stable between renders?
opts: Yes, it is the same function for the component's whole life
why: That is why it is safe to omit from effect deps and to pass down.

try.task: Write a pure cartReducer(state, action) with actions add (by id, increase qty if present), remove, setQty (remove at qty 0) and clear, plus a selector cartTotal(state). State: { items: [{ id, price, qty }] }.
try.hint: switch on action.type; map/filter to create new arrays; default: return state.

checks.t: setQty 0 removes; remove and clear work
pure: never mutates, unknown actions return the same state

takeaway.key: useReducer = one pure (state, action) → newState function. Return new objects; return the same state for "no change". Test the reducer without React.
mistakes: Mutating state in the reducer.
Side effects (fetch) inside the reducer.

dryRun.title: <ThemeContext value={{ theme, toggle }}> around the app
rows: yes, if the value is a NEW object
components that do not read the context
dryRun.note: Context passes a value deep down without prop drilling. Every component that reads it re-renders when the value changes by Object.is. An object literal is new on every render, so memoize the value (or split contexts).

think.q:
const Ctx = createContext('default')
function Show() { return <p>{useContext(Ctx)}</p> }
why: Without a provider above it, a consumer gets the default value. In React 19 you can render <Ctx> directly as the provider.

think.q:
const Ctx = createContext(null)
let renders = 0
const Reader = memo(function Reader() { useContext(Ctx); renders++; return null })
function App() { const [n, setN] = useState(0); return <Ctx value={{ user: 'a' }}><Reader /><button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>x</button></Ctx> }
why: The value object is new on every App render, so the memo-wrapped reader re-renders anyway.

think.q:
const Ctx = createContext(null)
let renders = 0
const Reader = memo(function Reader() { useContext(Ctx); renders++; return null })
function App() { const [n, setN] = useState(0); const value = useMemo(() => ({ user: 'a' }), []); return <Ctx value={value}><Reader /><button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>x</button></Ctx> }
why: A memoized value keeps its identity, so the reader is skipped.

think.q: What is context NOT a good fit for?
opts: Fast-changing state read by many components (e.g. mouse position)
why: Every change re-renders every consumer. Use a store with selectors for hot state.

think.q: Why throw in useTheme() when the context value is null?
opts: It turns a missing provider into a clear error instead of a confusing undefined later
why: A custom hook is the right place for that check.

try.task: Write ThemeProvider (holds "light"/"dark", memoizes its value) and useTheme() returning { theme, toggle }; useTheme must throw Error("useTheme must be used inside ThemeProvider") outside a provider.
try.hint: createContext(null); useState("light"); useMemo(() => ({ theme, toggle }), [theme]); in useTheme: if (!ctx) throw.

checks.t: toggle switches the theme for every consumer

takeaway.key: Context removes prop drilling; every consumer re-renders when the value changes. Memoize the value, wrap it in a guarded custom hook, keep hot state elsewhere.
mistakes: A new object as the value on every render.
Expecting memo() to block context updates.

think.q: When is useMemo NOT worth it?
opts: For a 50 ms sort of 20,000 rows
For an object passed to a memo() child
For a value used as an effect dependency
For cheap calculations like adding two numbers or a short filter
why: Memoization itself costs memory and comparisons. Measure first (React DevTools Profiler).

think.q: What does the React Compiler change about useMemo?
opts: It can memoize automatically, so many manual useMemo/useCallback calls become unnecessary
why: Still useful to understand what it does and why.

try.task: Write FilteredList({ items, query, filterFn }) that shows items matching the query in <li>s, computing the list with filterFn(items, query) inside useMemo so unrelated re-renders do not call it again.

checks.t: does not recompute for the same inputs

takeaway.key: useMemo caches a value until deps change (by reference). Use it for expensive work or stable references, after measuring.
mistakes: New arrays/objects as deps defeating the cache.
Memoizing trivial calculations.

think.q: When does useCallback do nothing useful?
opts: When the function is an effect dependency
When the function is passed to a normal (non-memo) element like a button
why: A DOM element does not care about function identity.

think.q: useCallback(fn, deps) is the same as…
why: useMemo(fn) would CALL fn and cache its result.

try.task: Write useStableCallback(fn): return a function whose identity never changes, but which always calls the latest fn (no stale closures).
examples: same identity every render; uses the newest draft
try.hint: Keep fn in a ref updated in useLayoutEffect (or useEffect); return useCallback((...a) => ref.current(...a), []).

dryRun.title: useLocalStorage("theme", "light") in two components
rows: B does not see it until it reads again
lift it up or use context/a store
dryRun.note: A custom hook is a function starting with "use" that calls other hooks. It shares logic, not state: each component that calls it gets its own copy. Name it for what it does (useDebouncedValue, useOnline), return what callers need.

think.q:
function useCounter() { const [n, setN] = useState(0); return [n, () => setN((x) => x + 1)] }

think.q: Why must a custom hook start with "use"?
opts: So React and the lint rules know it may call hooks and check the rules inside it
why: A function without the prefix that calls hooks hides the rule-breaking.

think.q: When should a hook return a tuple [value, set] vs an object?
opts: Tuple for 2 values callers will rename; object when there are more or names matter
why: useState style vs { data, error, loading }.

takeaway.key: Custom hooks share logic, not state. Prefix with use, keep the rules of hooks inside, test with renderHook.
mistakes: Expecting two components to share state through a custom hook.
